q: Why start a script with #!/usr/bin/env bash rather than #!/bin/bash?
choices: env finds the bash in your PATH, newer than the Mac's 3.2
It makes the script run faster
env runs the script as root
explain: The shebang names the program that reads the script. /bin/bash is a fixed path: on a Mac it is bash 3.2, from 2006. env looks bash up in your PATH, where a newer bash you installed comes first.

q: The template has die() { printf '%s: %s\n' "${0##*/}" "$*" >&2; exit 1; }. Why the >&2?
choices: Errors go to stderr, apart from the results
It writes the error into a file named 2
explain: >&2 sends the message to stderr, the error stream. The results (stdout) can then go into a file or a pipe while the error still reaches the screen or a log, and exit 1 tells the caller it failed.

q: At the prompt, ls *.log | wc -l is fine. Why not in a script?
choices: A name with a line break inside counts as two
explain: ls prints names as text, one per line, for your eyes. A name can hold a line break, and wc -l then counts it twice. At the prompt you would notice; a script keeps the names themselves, in an array: logs=(./*.log).

q: name='-n'. What does echo "$name" print?
choices: Nothing: echo takes -n for its option
explain: echo reads its first word as an option when it looks like one. -n means 'no newline', so there is nothing left to print. printf '%s\n' "$name" prints -n, since printf never takes its values for options.

q: Why does a script write cd /srv/app || exit 1, and not just cd /srv/app?
choices: If cd fails, the next lines don't run in the wrong folder
Without it, cd only works as root
explain: A script doesn't stop when a command fails. If /srv/app is missing, the next line, rm -rf ./cache for example, runs in whatever folder the script was in. || exit 1 stops it right there.

q: What does -- mean in rm -- "$f"?
choices: No options after it: $f is a name, even starting with -
Remove the folder and its content
explain: A file can be called -rf. Without --, rm would read that name as options. -- ends the options: whatever follows is a name. Most commands understand it.

q: Why does a script create its temp file with mktemp?
choices: It makes a new private file, with a name nobody can guess
/tmp only accepts files made by mktemp
explain: /tmp is shared by every user. A fixed name like /tmp/report.tmp can be created first by someone else, or made a link to one of your files. mktemp picks a random name, creates the file for you only, and prints its name. It doesn't remove it: a trap does that.

q: Your script goes wrong half way. What shows you each line as it runs, with its values?
explain: bash -x prints each line, after expansion, before running it, with a + in front: you see the values the variables really had. bash -n only checks the syntax and runs nothing.

q: In a script, which line counts the .log files of the folder, whatever their names?
explain: The array holds the names themselves, one item each, and ${#logs[@]} counts them. nullglob makes the pattern give nothing when no file matches. The others count words or lines of text: a space or a line break in a name, or no match at all, gives a wrong number.

q: set -e is on and count=0. What does ((count++)) do?
choices: It stops the script: (( )) saw 0, which counts as a failure
count becomes 1 and the script goes on
explain: count++ gives the old value, 0, then adds one. For (( )), 0 is false, so the command 'fails' and set -e stops the script, with no message. count=$((count + 1)) never fails.

q: local out=$(backup_db) || die "backup failed". backup_db fails. What happens?
choices: die never runs: the status is local's, and local worked
die runs and the script stops
explain: local is a command too, and its own status replaces backup_db's. Declare first, then assign: local out; out=$(backup_db) || die "backup failed". export and readonly hide the failure the same way.

q: for f in "$dir"/*.jpg runs on a folder with no .jpg. How many turns does the loop take?
choices: One, with f holding the pattern itself
One per file of the folder
explain: When no file matches, bash keeps the pattern as it is: the loop turns once, on a name that doesn't exist. shopt -s nullglob gives an empty list instead, or test [[ -e $f ]] || continue inside the loop.

q: while IFS= read -r host; do ssh "$host" uptime; done < hosts.txt only checks the first host. Why?
choices: ssh reads the loop's input and swallows the rest of the list
hosts.txt needs one more blank line
explain: Commands inside the loop share its standard input: the list. ssh reads all it can, to pass it on to the remote command, so read finds nothing left. ssh -n, or < /dev/null on that line, keeps it away.

q: Why printf '%s\n' "$x" rather than printf "$x\n"?
choices: A % inside x would be read as part of the format
explain: printf's first argument is a format: %s, %d and friends are replaced by the values after it. If the data is the format, a value like 50% breaks it. The format stays fixed, the data comes after.

q: b='*.txt'. What does [[ $a == $b ]] compare?
explain: On the right of == inside [[ ]], an unquoted value is a pattern. [[ $a == "$b" ]], with quotes, compares the exact text. Quote it unless you mean a pattern.

q: Why remove a temp file with trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT rather than an rm on the last line?
choices: The trap also runs when the script stops early
rm can't remove files made by mktemp
The last line never runs in bash
explain: An rm on the last line only runs when everything went well. A trap on EXIT runs however the script ends: the last line, an exit or a die half way, Ctrl+C. Not kill -9: nothing runs then.

q: set -o pipefail is on. Which pipeline can fail even though each command did its job?
explain: head stops reading after one line, and the next write of yes gets SIGPIPE: status 141. With pipefail, that makes the whole pipeline fail. Turn pipefail on where you check pipes, and remember this case.

q: Which loop handles every file of a tree, even names with line breaks?
choices: find . -type f | while read f; do …; done
explain: -print0 ends each name with a zero byte, the one character a name can't hold, and read -d '' cuts exactly there. The others cut text at spaces or line breaks. find -exec cmd {} + is the other safe way.

q: n comes from the user. Why check [[ $n =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] before (( n > 5 ))?
choices: (( )) reads n as code: x[$(date)] would run date
explain: Arithmetic evaluates what the variable holds, array indexes included, and an index can hold a command substitution. Checking that the value is digits first keeps input from deciding what runs. Then write (( 10#$n > 5 )): a leading 0 makes (( )) read octal, and 08 is an error.

q: rm -rf -- "${dir:?}"/* runs with dir empty. What happens?
choices: The script stops with an error, before rm runs
explain: ${dir:?} stops the script with 'dir: parameter null or not set' when dir is empty or unset. Without it, the line would be rm -rf -- /*: rm refuses / itself, but not everything in it. A typo in a variable name is enough to empty it.

q: n=0; grep x f | while read -r l; do n=$((n + 1)); done; printf '%s\n' "$n" prints 0. Why?
choices: The loop ran in a subshell: its n is gone after the pipe
printf prints the first value n had
explain: Each part of a pipeline runs in its own subshell, the while loop too: it counts in a copy of n. Feed it with process substitution instead, and the loop runs in the script itself: while …; done < <(grep x f).

q: A script runs sed "s/$old/$new/" file, and new holds a/b. What happens?
choices: Its / ends the expression: an error, or a wrong change
explain: The value becomes part of sed's program, so its characters are code there: /, & and \ mean something. Escape them first, or pass data to a program that takes it as data, like awk through the environment: new=$new awk '{ … ENVIRON["new"] … }' (-v would still turn backslashes into escapes).

q: Two copies of a script must never run at once. Which lock is safe?
choices: touch lock, then check that it exists
A variable LOCKED=1 at the top
explain: mkdir creates the folder or fails, in one step: two copies can't both succeed. With a test then a touch, both copies can pass the test before either creates the file. flock is the other safe tool on Linux. Remove the lock however the script ends: trap 'rmdir -- "$lock"' EXIT, right after mkdir worked. After a kill -9 it stays: remove it by hand.

q: Why does sort data.txt > data.txt leave data.txt empty?
choices: The shell empties data.txt for > before sort reads it
explain: Redirections happen before the command starts: > truncates data.txt, then sort reads an empty file. Write to another file, then move it: sort data.txt > data.tmp && mv data.tmp data.txt (or sort -o data.txt data.txt, which sort handles).
